blocks.text: **The problem.** Given the `root` of a binary tree, return the values of its nodes in **preorder**, **inorder** and **postorder**. (On LeetCode these are three separate questions — 144, 94 and 145 — but they are one idea, so they share one lesson.)

blocks.alt: The tree 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, null, 6 and its three traversals. Preorder (root, left, right): 1 2 4 5 3 6. Inorder (left, root, right): 4 2 5 1 3 6. Postorder (left, right, root): 4 5 2 6 3 1.

blocks.text: All three are **depth-first**: go all the way down the left side before the right side. The only difference is **when** you write down the node — the name says where the root goes: **pre** = before its subtrees, **in** = in between them, **post** = after them.

Each order has a job. **Preorder** copies or serializes a tree (you meet the root first, so you can rebuild it). **Inorder** of a binary search tree gives the values in **sorted order**. **Postorder** handles children before parents — deleting a tree, or computing sizes and heights.

Picture the recursive walk tracing around the outside of the tree. It passes every node **three times**: arriving from above, coming back up from the left subtree, and coming back up from the right subtree. Write the value at the first pass for preorder, the second for inorder, the third for postorder.

blocks.alt: A dashed line traces around the outside of the tree, starting at the root and going down the left side first. Each node is passed three times: before its left subtree (preorder), between its subtrees (inorder) and after its right subtree (postorder).

blocks.caption: All three arrays fill in during the same walk — watch which pass writes to which.

blocks.text: The definitions translate straight into code. Only the position of the "visit" line changes:

blocks.code:
def preorder_traversal(root, out=None):
    out = [] if out is None else out
    if root:
        out.append(root.val)                    # root
        preorder_traversal(root.left, out)      # left
        preorder_traversal(root.right, out)     # right
    return out

def inorder_traversal(root, out=None):
    out = [] if out is None else out
    if root:
        inorder_traversal(root.left, out)       # left
        out.append(root.val)                    # root
        inorder_traversal(root.right, out)      # right
    return out

def postorder_traversal(root, out=None):
    out = [] if out is None else out
    if root:
        postorder_traversal(root.left, out)     # left
        postorder_traversal(root.right, out)    # right
        out.append(root.val)                    # root
    return out

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(h)** for the call stack — up to O(n) for a skewed tree, which can overflow the call stack on very deep inputs. Interviewers often follow up: *now do it without recursion*.

items: **Preorder** — pop a node, visit it, push its **right** child and then its **left** child (so the left is popped first).
**Inorder** — keep walking **left**, pushing every node. When you can't go further, pop, visit, and then step into that node's **right** subtree.
**Postorder** — the trick: run preorder with the children pushed in the opposite order (**root, right, left**), then **reverse** the result to get left, right, root.

blocks.alt: Iterative inorder on the tree 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Walk left from 1 to 2 to 4, pushing each. Pop 4 and visit it; it has no right child. Pop 2 and visit it, then step right to 5.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(h)** for the stack — the same as recursion, but it can't overflow the call stack, and it's the version interviewers ask for.
3. Best solution: Morris traversal, O(1) extra space

Both versions above remember the way back up in a stack. **Morris traversal** remembers it **inside the tree**. Before going down into a node's left subtree, find that subtree's **rightmost** node (the node visited just before this one in inorder) and point its empty `right` link back up to the current node — a temporary **thread**. When the walk later arrives through the thread, it knows the left side is finished, removes the thread, and moves right. Every thread is removed, so the tree ends up unchanged.

blocks.alt: Morris threading. Before descending into 1's left subtree, the rightmost node of that subtree, 5, gets a temporary right link back to 1. After visiting 5, the walk follows the thread back to 1, removes it, and continues to 3.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1).** Finding predecessors walks some edges twice, but every edge is walked at most a constant number of times overall. The catch: the tree is modified *during* the walk, so it isn't safe if another thread reads the tree at the same time. (A Morris postorder exists too, but it's fiddly; in interviews, the iterative version is the usual answer.)

rows.spaceWhy: The call stack: up to O(n) for a **skewed** tree.

rows.timeWhy: Every node is **pushed and popped once**.
rows.spaceWhy: An explicit stack of **one path**, which can't overflow the call stack.

rows.timeWhy: Finding predecessors walks each edge **a constant number of times**.
rows.spaceWhy: It threads through the tree's **empty right pointers** instead of a stack.

items: **A left-only chain** — `[3, 2, null, 1]`: preorder 3 2 1, inorder 1 2 3, postorder 1 2 3.
**A right-only chain** — `[1, null, 2, null, 3]`: recursion depth equals n.
**N-ary Tree Preorder / Postorder Traversal** — the same orders with a list of children instead of two.
**Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder** — preorder names the root; inorder splits the rest into the left and right subtrees.
**Validate Binary Search Tree / Kth Smallest Element in a BST** — an inorder walk of a BST visits values in sorted order.
